exam.q: Explain two ways in which the belief that God is loving influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christians try to copy God's love by showing agape, selfless love, to others. Since they believe God loves everyone, they volunteer at food banks, support charities and help people regardless of who they are. A second way is that it gives them comfort and confidence in prayer. Because they believe God loves them and sent his Son to save them, they turn to him in hard times, trusting that he cares and will forgive them when they are truly sorry.
points: Christians copy God's love through selfless service (agape), e.g. charity work
Belief in God's love gives comfort and encourages prayer
God's love shown in sending Jesus gives confidence in forgiveness
Love for all encourages Christians to treat everyone equally and forgive enemies

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the problem of evil and suffering influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it motivates Christians to reduce suffering. If God allows suffering, Christians believe they should act as his hands, so they work for charities such as Christian Aid and help the sick and poor. A second way is that it can test or change their faith. Some Christians trust that God has a plan and pray for strength, while others struggle with doubt and ask how a loving, powerful God could allow innocent people to suffer.
points: Motivates practical action to help those who suffer
Encourages trust in God's plan and prayer
May cause doubt or loss of faith
Linked to free will, the Devil or testing: Christians respond by resisting evil

exam.q: Explain two ways in which a belief in the crucifixion influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it gives Christians confidence that they can be forgiven. They believe Jesus died as a sacrifice for human sin, so they can ask God for forgiveness and try to forgive others. A second way is that it helps Christians cope with suffering. They believe Jesus suffered pain and death too, so God understands what they go through, and many find comfort looking at a cross or crucifix when they pray.
points: Forgiveness of sins is possible and Christians should forgive others
God understands human suffering because Jesus suffered
Sign of the cross, crucifix and Good Friday services remind Christians of sacrifice
Shows God's love, so Christians try to love sacrificially

exam.q: Explain two ways in which a belief in life after death influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it gives Christians hope when someone dies. They believe that people who have faith will live on with God, so funerals are services of hope and Christians are comforted knowing they will be reunited with loved ones. A second way is that it encourages them to live as God wants. They believe that how they live now affects what happens after death, so they try to follow Jesus' teachings, such as helping the poor.
points: Gives hope and comfort at funerals and bereavement
Reduces fear of death
Encourages moral living as this life prepares for the next
Influences how funerals and prayers for the dead are conducted

exam.q: Explain two ways in which a belief in the final judgement influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it encourages Christians to behave morally. They believe God will judge the living and the dead, so they try to obey the Ten Commandments and avoid sin. A second way is that it motivates them to help others. The parable of the sheep and the goats teaches that people will be judged on how they treated the hungry, sick and imprisoned, so many Christians give to charity and volunteer.
points: Encourages moral living because God will judge
Motivates charity and service, e.g. sheep and goats
Gives hope that justice will be done
Encourages repentance and asking for forgiveness

exam.q: Explain two ways in which a belief in hell influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it encourages Christians to follow God's teachings. If hell is separation from God, they want to avoid it, so they try to live as Jesus taught. A second way is that it encourages them to treat others well. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows a man who ignored a poor beggar ending up in torment, so Christians help the poor and avoid selfishness.
points: Motivates living by God's commands to avoid separation from God
Encourages care for the poor and others (Lazarus parable)
Encourages evangelism to save others
Some Christians emphasise God's mercy, so focus on repentance

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about the Trinity. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that there is one God who exists as three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This means the three are equal and eternal but not three gods. In the Nicene Creed Christians say they believe in 'one God' and in the Father, Son and Spirit. This shows that Christians worship one God in three persons. Another belief is that each person has a role. The Son became human in Jesus to save humanity and the Spirit guides believers. At Jesus' baptism the Father's voice said 'You are my Son' and the Spirit came like a dove (Mark 1:11). This shows all three together. So Christians baptise in the name of the Trinity.
points: One God in three persons: Father, Son, Holy Spirit
Equal, eternal, not three gods
Each person has a role: Father creates, Son saves, Spirit guides
Sources: Nicene Creed, Matthew 28:19, Mark 1:9-11, Deuteronomy 6:4
Application: baptism and worship in the name of the Trinity

exam.q: Explain two different Christian beliefs about creation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that God created the world exactly as described in Genesis 1, in six days. Some Christians, such as creationists, take the Bible literally because they believe it is God's word. Genesis 1:1 says 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth'. This means they reject evolution and believe God made humans in his image. A different belief is that Genesis is not literal but teaches that God made the world and why. Many Catholics and Anglicans accept the Big Bang and evolution as the way God created. John 1:1-3 says that through the Word, Jesus, all things were made. This means that creation is about God's purpose rather than a science textbook, so Christians can accept science and still care for the world as stewards.
points: Literal: six days, Genesis 1:1, fundamentalists
Non-literal: Genesis a story with meaning; compatible with Big Bang
Sources: Genesis 1:1-3, John 1:1-3, Genesis 1:27
Application: stewardship, rejecting or accepting evolution
Role of Word and Spirit may be credited

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about Jesus as the Son of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin, which shows he had a special relationship with God. In Luke 1:35 the angel tells Mary 'the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God'. This means Christians believe Jesus was God in human form, the incarnation. Another belief is that God the Father declared Jesus his Son at his baptism. In Mark 1:11 a voice from heaven says 'You are my Son, whom I love'. This means Christians believe Jesus is part of the Trinity and so his teachings have divine authority, so they follow what he said.
points: Virgin conception by the Holy Spirit
God's voice at baptism
Jesus fully God and fully human; part of the Trinity
Sources: Luke 1:35, Mark 1:11, John 1:14, Matthew 1:23
Application: Jesus' teaching is authoritative; Christmas celebrates the incarnation

exam.q: Explain two reasons why the resurrection of Jesus is important for Christians. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One reason is that it shows Jesus is the Son of God and has power over death. Christians believe God raised him from the dead, which proves his teaching was true. In Luke 24:5-6 the angels tell the women at the empty tomb 'He is not here; he has risen!' This means Christians can trust Jesus and celebrate Easter as the most important festival. A second reason is that it gives believers hope of life after death. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:20 that Christ has been raised as 'the first fruits of those who are asleep'. This means Christians believe they too will be raised, so they face death with hope.
points: Proves Jesus is the Son of God and victorious over death and sin
Gives hope of resurrection and eternal life
Sources: Luke 24:5-6, 1 Corinthians 15:14 or 15:20, Apostles' Creed
Application: celebrating Easter; funerals as hope

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about how salvation can be achieved. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that salvation comes through grace. This means it is a free gift from God that cannot be earned. Many Protestants believe this because Ephesians 2:8-9 says 'it is by grace you have been saved, through faith'. This means Christians trust in Jesus' sacrifice rather than relying on good deeds. Another belief is that salvation also needs good works or following God's law. James 2:17 says 'faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead'. Catholics teach that faith and good works go together, so Christians help the poor and keep the commandments to show their faith is real.
points: Grace: free gift from God, through faith
Law and works: following commandments, good deeds
Spirit: Holy Spirit works in believers (Galatians 5:22-23, Titus 3:5)
Sources: Ephesians 2:8-9, James 2:17, Romans 3:28
Application: trust in Jesus; charity and obeying commandments

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about the role of Jesus in salvation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that Jesus' death was an atoning sacrifice that restored the relationship between God and humans. Sin had separated people from God, but 1 John 2:2 says Jesus 'is the atoning sacrifice for our sins'. This means Christians believe Jesus paid the price for sin, so they can be forgiven, which is why they confess their sins and take Holy Communion. Another belief is that Jesus' resurrection defeated sin and death and made eternal life possible. John 3:16 says that whoever believes in him 'shall not perish but have eternal life'. This means Christians have hope of heaven and try to live faithfully.
points: Atonement: sacrifice restoring relationship
Resurrection defeated sin and death; eternal life
Jesus the 'way' to the Father (John 14:6)
Sources: 1 John 2:2, John 3:16, Romans 5:10, Mark 10:45
Application: forgiveness, Communion, hope of heaven

exam.q: 'The existence of evil and suffering shows that God cannot be all-powerful and loving.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: If God is omnipotent he could stop evil, and if he is omnibenevolent he would want to, but children suffer from disease and disasters, so one of these must be false (the inconsistent triad).
Natural evil, such as earthquakes, is not caused by humans, so free will cannot explain it. This challenges a just God.
The Bible shows God stopping evil at times, such as the plagues in Egypt, so why not now?
against: Free will: God gave humans choice, because love must be freely given. Moral evil comes from human choices, not God. Genesis 3 shows the Fall.
The Devil tempts people (1 Peter 5:8), so evil comes from Satan.
Suffering can test and strengthen faith. Romans 8:28 says God works for good in all things, and humans cannot see the whole plan, as in Job.
Jesus suffered on the cross, so God shares our pain.
exam.conclusion: The statement is a strong challenge, but the free will response is more convincing for moral evil, though natural evil remains hard. Christians can reasonably keep belief in a loving, powerful God while admitting mystery.
exam.model:
Many people agree with this statement. If God is omnipotent, he could stop evil, and if he is omnibenevolent, he would want to. Yet innocent children suffer from disease and natural disasters like tsunamis. This is called the inconsistent triad, and it suggests that God cannot be both all-powerful and all-loving. Natural evil is a particular problem, because humans do not cause it, so free will cannot be blamed. This argument is strong because it uses simple logic and real examples of suffering. However, it assumes that a loving God would stop all suffering, which Christians dispute.

Christians have several responses. First, God gave humans free will. Love needs freedom, so people can choose evil, and this causes moral evil. Genesis 3 shows Adam and Eve misusing their freedom, bringing sin and suffering into the world. This response works well for crimes like murder, but less well for natural disasters. Some Christians add that Satan tempts people (1 Peter 5:8) and that suffering can test faith or help people grow. Romans 8:28 says that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, which suggests humans cannot see the whole plan, as in the book of Job. This is weaker for non-believers because it relies on faith, but for Christians it is convincing. Also, belief in the crucifixion shows God shares human suffering, so a loving God does not abandon people.

In conclusion, the statement is a powerful challenge, especially about natural evil. However, I think the Christian responses are strong enough to show God could still be loving and powerful, because free will explains much human evil and Jesus' suffering shows God cares. The problem remains difficult, but it does not prove God cannot be both.

exam.q: 'The Genesis creation account is the best explanation of how the universe began.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Bible is the word of God, so Genesis 1 is true. Fundamentalists believe God created the world in six days.
It explains why the world exists and gives humans value as made in God's image (Genesis 1:27).
Science cannot explain what caused the Big Bang or why there is something rather than nothing; Genesis gives a creator.
against: Science (the Big Bang and evolution) is supported by evidence such as fossils and observation of expanding space, which Genesis cannot match.
Many Christians read Genesis as symbolic: 'day' may not mean 24 hours, and the story teaches why God made the world, not how.
Catholics and Anglicans accept evolution as God's method. John 1:1-3 says all things were made through the Word, which is compatible with the Big Bang.
exam.conclusion: Genesis is the best explanation of why the universe exists, but not of how it began. Most Christians combine faith and science.
exam.model:
Some Christians agree with this statement. Fundamentalists and creationists believe the Bible is the inspired word of God, so Genesis 1 is a true record: God created the world in six days and made humans in his image (Genesis 1:27). They argue that science cannot explain what began the Big Bang or why anything exists, while Genesis names God as the cause. Genesis also explains why humans are valuable and should be stewards of the earth. This argument is strong for those who accept the Bible as completely true, but it is weak for people who do not already believe in it, because it depends on faith rather than evidence.

Other people disagree. Scientific theories such as the Big Bang and evolution are supported by evidence like fossils and the expansion of the universe. Many Christians therefore read Genesis as a symbolic story. The Hebrew word for 'day' may mean a long period, and the story teaches that God is the creator and that creation is good, not how it happened. The Catholic Church accepts evolution as a possible way God created, and the Church of England is similar. John 1:1-3 says all things were made through the Word, which allows Christians to say God worked through natural processes. This argument is persuasive because it keeps faith and science together and avoids rejecting strong evidence.

In conclusion, I think Genesis is not the best explanation of how the universe began, because science gives detailed evidence, but it is a powerful answer to why the universe exists and what humans are for. Many Christians accept both, which is the most balanced view.

exam.q: 'The resurrection is the most important belief for Christians.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Without the resurrection, Christian faith would be pointless (1 Corinthians 15:14).
It proves Jesus is the Son of God and that his death defeated sin.
It gives hope of life after death and is celebrated at Easter and every Sunday.
against: The crucifixion is the sacrifice that atones for sin, so it is equally or more important.
The incarnation and Trinity are the foundation: without God becoming human, there is no saviour.
Some Christians stress living by Jesus' teaching and love of neighbour over any single belief.
exam.conclusion: The resurrection is central because it confirms everything else, but the beliefs are closely linked; it is arguably the most important because it validates the others.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:14 that if Christ has not been raised, preaching and faith are useless. The resurrection proves that Jesus is the Son of God and that his death defeated sin and death. It also gives Christians hope that they will have eternal life, as the Apostles' Creed says 'I believe in the resurrection of the body'. Easter is the most important festival, and many Christians worship on Sunday to remember it. This argument is strong because it explains why the early Church began and why Christians face death with confidence.

However, others argue that other beliefs are as important or more so. The crucifixion is where atonement happens: Jesus' sacrifice paid for human sin, as 1 John 2:2 says. Without it, there would be nothing for the resurrection to confirm. Some also say the incarnation is most important, because unless God became human in Jesus, there could be no saviour who is both God and human. Others stress the Trinity, or Jesus' teaching, such as loving your neighbour (Mark 12:31), and say Christianity is about how people live. This argument is persuasive because the beliefs depend on each other, so it is hard to rank them.

In conclusion, I think the resurrection is the most important belief because it confirms Jesus' identity and his sacrifice, and gives Christians hope. The crucifixion matters hugely, but without the resurrection it would look like a tragic defeat. The statement is therefore largely convincing, though the beliefs are best seen as a whole.

exam.q: 'A loving God would not send anyone to hell.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: God is omnibenevolent, and eternal punishment seems unfair for finite sins.
Jesus taught forgiveness and told parables like the prodigal son, showing God welcomes anyone who returns (Luke 15).
Some Christians, such as universalists, believe God's love will eventually save everyone, and others see hell as a symbol.
against: God is also just, and justice requires punishment for evil. Matthew 25:46 speaks of eternal punishment.
Humans have free will, so people who reject God choose separation themselves; God does not 'send' anyone.
Hell is taught by the Creeds and Jesus' parables, such as the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16), as a warning to live well.
exam.conclusion: The strongest view is that God's love and justice both matter: hell is better understood as a choice to be separated from God, so a loving God does not send people, but allows them to choose.
exam.model:
Some Christians agree with the statement. They argue that God is omnibenevolent, so eternal punishment for sins committed in a short life seems unfair and cruel. Jesus taught forgiveness, and in the parable of the prodigal son the father welcomes his son home whatever he has done (Luke 15). Some Christians, such as universalists, believe that God's love will eventually bring everyone to him, and some see hell as a symbol rather than a place. This argument is strong because it fits the idea that God is love (1 John 4:8), but it is weaker because it ignores Jesus' warnings.

Other Christians disagree. God is not only loving but also just, and a just God must deal with evil. Matthew 25:46 says the unrighteous will go away to eternal punishment, and the parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows a man suffering because he ignored the poor. The Creeds also speak of judgement. Many Christians argue that humans have free will, so those who reject God choose to be separated from him; God does not so much send them as allow their choice. This argument is convincing because it protects both love and freedom. It also gives people a reason to take morality seriously.

In conclusion, I think the second view is stronger. A loving God can still allow hell as the result of people freely rejecting him, and justice would be meaningless if cruelty had no consequences. However, the first view reminds Christians to stress God's mercy and to avoid claiming to know who is in hell. So the statement is partly true, but it oversimplifies.

exam.q: 'Good works are more important than faith for Christians who want to be saved.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: James 2:17 says faith without action is dead, so works prove faith is real.
In the sheep and goats parable (Matthew 25:31-46) people are judged on how they treat others, not on belief.
Catholics teach that faith and works together lead to salvation; the Old Testament law shows God expects obedience.
against: Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is by grace through faith, not works, so no one can boast.
Paul says in Romans 3:28 that people are justified by faith, not by keeping the law.
Humans always sin, so no amount of good works could earn heaven; only Jesus' sacrifice and God's grace can save.
exam.conclusion: Faith and works are linked, but grace through faith comes first, so works are the fruit of faith rather than more important than it.
exam.model:
Some Christians agree with this statement. James 2:17 says faith without action is dead, so a person who claims to believe but does nothing is not truly saved. In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25), the people are judged on how they treated the hungry, sick and imprisoned, which suggests works matter greatly. Catholics teach that faith and good works together lead to salvation, and the Old Testament law shows that God expects obedience. This argument is strong because it fits Jesus' emphasis on caring for others and it stops faith becoming empty words.

Other Christians disagree, especially Protestants. Ephesians 2:8-9 says that people are saved by grace through faith, 'not by works, so that no one can boast'. Paul says in Romans 3:28 that people are justified by faith, not by keeping the law. Because all people sin (Romans 3:23), no one could ever do enough good works to earn eternal life; only Jesus' sacrifice can save them. On this view, good works are the result of being saved, not the cause. This argument is convincing because it explains why even someone who has done many bad things can still be forgiven, and it stresses God's generosity.

In conclusion, I think the second view is stronger because salvation is a gift and faith comes first. However, James shows that real faith will produce action, so works are not unimportant. The statement is therefore not fully correct: faith and works are linked, but works are best seen as the evidence of faith rather than more important than it.

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about the nature of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that God is omnipotent, which means all-powerful. Christians believe God created the whole universe and can do anything that is not against his nature, so they believe he can answer prayer and work miracles. Jesus taught 'with God all things are possible' (Matthew 19:26). This means Christians trust God even when a situation seems hopeless. A second belief is that God is loving (omnibenevolent). Christians believe God cares for every person and wants the best for them, even those who reject him. The First Letter of John says simply 'God is love' (1 John 4:8), and John 3:16 says God gave his only Son to save the world. This means Christians believe the greatest proof of God's love is Jesus' death on the cross, and they try to show the same selfless agape love to others.
points: Omnipotent: all-powerful, creator, can answer prayer and do miracles
Loving / omnibenevolent: cares for all, shown in sending Jesus
Just: fair judge who rewards good and punishes evil
One God in three persons (Trinity)
Sources: Matthew 19:26, Luke 1:37, 1 John 4:8, John 3:16, Micah 6:8, Ecclesiastes 3:17
Application: e.g. 'This means Christians trust God in hard times' or 'so they show agape love'

exam.q: 'God's love is more important than God's justice.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Many Christians would agree with this statement. The First Letter of John says 'God is love' (1 John 4:8), which describes God's very nature, not just one thing he does. John 3:16 teaches that God's love was the reason he sent Jesus to save the world. Jesus taught people to love even their enemies, and in the parable of the prodigal son the father runs to welcome his son home before the son has even finished apologising (Luke 15). This suggests that mercy and love come first. This argument is strong because the whole Christian story of salvation begins with God's love, and Christians are told to copy that love through agape.

However, other Christians argue that God's justice is just as important. The Bible often describes God as a fair judge: 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked' (Ecclesiastes 3:17). In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25), people face real consequences for ignoring the hungry and poor. If God only loved and never judged, evil people would never face consequences, and their victims would never see justice done. This argument is also strong, because a love that ignored cruelty would not really be love for the victims.

Many Christians would say the two cannot be separated. At the crucifixion God's justice takes sin seriously, because sin has a real cost, but God's love pays that cost himself through Jesus. Without justice, forgiveness would mean nothing, because there would be nothing to forgive. Without love, justice would leave everyone condemned, since 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23).

In conclusion, I think the statement is partly right. Love is arguably the deepest description of God, because the Bible says God 'is' love but does not say God 'is' justice in the same way. However, it is misleading to call one more important, because the cross shows that God's justice is an expression of his love for the world and especially for those who suffer injustice.
for: 1 John 4:8 says 'God is love', describing God's very nature.
God's love is the reason for salvation (John 3:16); the prodigal son shows mercy before punishment.
Jesus commanded love of enemies, so love seems to be the priority for Christian life.
against: God is a just judge (Ecclesiastes 3:17); the sheep and goats parable shows real consequences.
Without justice, evil would win and victims would never see wrongs put right.
Love and justice meet at the cross: sin has a cost and God's love pays it, so neither is more important.
exam.conclusion: Love is the deepest description of God, but the cross shows justice is part of God's love, so neither can be ranked above the other without distorting Christian teaching.

exam.q: Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil and suffering. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One response is free will. Christians believe God gave humans the freedom to choose, because real love must be freely chosen, and so people can also choose to do evil. In Genesis 3 Adam and Eve freely disobeyed God, and Paul says that through one man 'sin entered into the world' (Romans 5:12). This means moral evil such as murder is the fault of human choices, not God, so Christians try to use their own freedom well. A second response is that humans cannot fully understand God's plan. In the book of Job, a good man loses everything, but God does not explain why; instead he shows Job how limited human knowledge is. This means Christians trust God and pray for strength even when suffering seems pointless, believing as Romans 8:28 says that God works for good in all things.
points: Free will: love must be freely chosen; moral evil is caused by humans (Genesis 3, Romans 5:12)
The Devil tempts people to sin (1 Peter 5:8)
Soul-making: suffering helps people grow (Irenaeus)
Mystery / trust: humans cannot understand God's plan (Job; Romans 8:28)
God suffers with us: Jesus on the cross (Mark 15:34)
Application: e.g. 'so Christians help victims' or 'so they trust God in prayer'

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the Holy Spirit influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides them. Jesus promised the Spirit would teach and remind his followers, so before important decisions many Christians pray for the Spirit's guidance and read the Bible expecting the Spirit to help them understand it. A second way is that it gives them courage to share their faith. At Pentecost the Spirit turned frightened disciples into bold preachers, so Christians today believe the same Spirit helps them speak about Jesus to friends or support mission work, even when they feel nervous.
points: Guidance in decisions and understanding the Bible, so they pray for guidance
Comfort and strength in suffering, so they keep going and trust God
Courage to evangelise, as at Pentecost
Develop the fruit of the Spirit (love, patience, kindness) in how they treat others
Charismatic worship: speaking in tongues, healing prayer
Confirmation: receiving the Spirit to live as an adult Christian

exam.q: 'The Trinity is impossible to understand, so it is not important for Christians.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some people would agree with this statement. The idea that one God exists as three persons seems to break ordinary logic, because one cannot equal three. Even great Christian thinkers have called the Trinity a mystery, and the word 'Trinity' does not appear in the Bible. Some groups who call themselves Christian, such as Unitarians, reject the doctrine, and many ordinary Christians focus on following Jesus' teaching to love their neighbour rather than on complicated ideas. This argument has some strength: a belief that people cannot explain may seem less useful in everyday life than clear moral teaching.

However, most Christians strongly disagree. The Trinity is central to the Nicene Creed, which churches around the world say in worship, and it is how Christians understand who Jesus is. If Jesus were not God the Son, his death could not save humanity, and if the Holy Spirit were not God, Christians could not say God is with them today. Jesus told his followers to baptise 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19), so the Trinity is part of how every Christian life begins. This argument is stronger, because it shows the Trinity holds the rest of Christian belief together.

Christians would also say that being hard to understand does not make something unimportant. God is infinite, so it is not surprising that humans cannot fully grasp him. Christians experience God in three ways: as the Father who created them, the Son who saved them and the Spirit who guides them, and they pray 'to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit'. A mystery can still be true and meaningful.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. The Trinity is difficult, but the argument that it is unimportant confuses 'hard to explain' with 'unimportant'. The Trinity shapes baptism, worship, prayer and belief in salvation, so for most Christians it is essential.
for: One God in three persons seems illogical, and the word 'Trinity' is not in the Bible.
Some groups, such as Unitarians, reject it but still try to follow Jesus.
Many Christians focus on practical teaching like loving your neighbour rather than doctrine.
against: The Trinity is in the Nicene Creed and is said in worship worldwide.
Matthew 28:19: baptism is in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, so it begins every Christian life.
Salvation depends on Jesus being God the Son; God's presence today depends on the Spirit being God.
Being a mystery is expected for an infinite God and does not make it unimportant.
exam.conclusion: Difficult is not the same as unimportant. The Trinity underpins baptism, prayer, worship and salvation, so it is essential for most Christians.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief that God created the world influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christians act as stewards of the environment. Genesis teaches that God made the world and gave humans responsibility to look after it, so Christians recycle, reduce waste and support campaigns against climate change because they believe the earth belongs to God. A second way is that they value every human life. Christians believe God made humans in his own image, so they treat each person with respect, oppose things like racism and support charities that protect the vulnerable.
points: Stewardship: caring for the environment, e.g. recycling, climate campaigns
Sanctity of life: every person made in God's image, so respect and protect life
Worship and thankfulness: praise God as creator, e.g. harvest festivals
Some reject evolution and support creationist teaching; others see science as exploring God's work
Awe at nature leads to prayer and belief in God's power

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the incarnation influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christians treat Jesus' teaching as having God's own authority. Because they believe Jesus was God in human form, they follow what he said, for example forgiving others and helping the poor, rather than seeing him as just a good teacher. A second way is that it gives them comfort when they suffer. Christians believe that in Jesus God lived a real human life and felt hunger, grief and pain, so when they are going through hard times they pray knowing God understands exactly how they feel.
points: Jesus' teaching has divine authority, so Christians obey it
God understands human suffering, so Christians find comfort in prayer
Celebrate Christmas with worship, nativity services and generosity
Human life is valued highly because God became human, so Christians respect all people
Jesus is an example of how to live, so Christians try to imitate him

exam.q: 'Jesus was just a good human teacher, not the Son of God.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Jesus lived as a real human: he was born, grew up, felt hunger, cried at the death of his friend Lazarus and died on a cross. Non-religious people and some liberal thinkers admire his teaching on love and forgiveness, such as the parable of the Good Samaritan, without believing he was divine. They argue that stories like the virgin conception and miracles may have been added later to show how important he was. This argument is reasonable for someone who does not accept the Bible as reliable, but it does not explain why his followers were willing to die claiming he had risen.

Most Christians strongly disagree. They believe in the incarnation: 'The Word became flesh, and lived among us' (John 1:14). The angel told Mary that her child would be called 'the Son of God' (Luke 1:35), and at Jesus' baptism a voice from heaven said 'You are my Son' (Mark 1:11). Jesus forgave sins, which Jewish leaders said only God could do, and he accepted Thomas calling him 'My Lord and my God' (John 20:28). Most importantly, Christians believe God raised him from the dead, which a mere teacher could not explain.

Christians also argue that the statement does not hold together. C. S. Lewis pointed out that Jesus claimed to be one with the Father (John 10:30). If that claim was false, Jesus would not be a 'good teacher' but either deluded or dishonest. So either he was more than a teacher, or he was not good.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. A believer could not accept it, because the Creeds, the resurrection and the idea of salvation all depend on Jesus being the Son of God. Even for a non-believer, calling Jesus 'just a good teacher' is the weakest option, because it ignores the claims he made about himself.
for: Jesus lived a real human life and his moral teaching (e.g. Good Samaritan) can be admired without belief in God.
Some argue miracle and virgin birth stories were added later to show his importance.
Some liberal Christians focus on Jesus' example rather than his divinity.
against: John 1:14: the Word became flesh; Luke 1:35 and Mark 1:11 call him Son of God.
He forgave sins and accepted worship ('My Lord and my God', John 20:28).
The resurrection shows God's approval of his claims.
If his claims (John 10:30) were false he could not be a good teacher (C. S. Lewis' argument).
exam.conclusion: For Christians the statement fails because the Creeds and salvation depend on Jesus being God the Son; even logically, 'just a good teacher' sits badly with the claims Jesus made.

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about the crucifixion of Jesus. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that the crucifixion was part of God's plan to save humanity from sin. Jesus knew he would die and told his disciples beforehand that he would be killed and rise on the third day (Mark 9:31). Paul also says that 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3). This means Christians believe Jesus' death was a willing sacrifice, not a defeat, so they can be forgiven. A second belief is that the crucifixion teaches forgiveness. Even while in agony, Jesus prayed 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). This means Christians believe that no one is beyond forgiveness, and they try to forgive people who hurt them, even when it is very hard.
points: Part of God's plan; Jesus predicted it (Mark 9:31); fulfilled scripture (Isaiah 53:5, 1 Corinthians 15:3)
A sacrifice for sin making forgiveness possible
Teaches forgiveness: 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34)
God shares human suffering: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34)
Promise of paradise to the repentant criminal (Luke 23:43)
Nicene Creed: 'For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate'

exam.q: 'The crucifixion is more important for Christians than the resurrection.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. They believe the crucifixion is the moment when sin was dealt with. John the Baptist called Jesus 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29), and 1 John 2:2 calls him 'the atoning sacrifice for our sins'. Without his death there would be no atonement, and humans would remain separated from God. The cross is the main Christian symbol, Christians make the sign of the cross, and Holy Communion remembers Jesus' body broken and blood shed. Jesus' final words 'It is finished' (John 19:30) suggest that his work of salvation was completed on the cross. This argument is strong because it explains how forgiveness is possible.

Other Christians argue that the resurrection is more important. Paul wrote that 'if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:14). Many people were crucified by the Romans; what made Jesus different was that he rose again. The resurrection proves he was the Son of God, shows that death has been defeated and gives Christians hope of eternal life. It is why Easter is the greatest Christian festival and why Christians worship on Sunday. This argument is also strong, because without the resurrection the crucifixion would look like the failure of a good man.

However, the two events are really two halves of one act of salvation. The crucifixion deals with sin, and the resurrection defeats death and shows that the sacrifice was accepted by God. The Creeds put them side by side: he was crucified, died and was buried, and on the third day he rose again.

In conclusion, I think the resurrection is slightly more important, because it gives meaning to the crucifixion and is what Paul says the faith stands or falls on. However, most Christians would say it is a mistake to separate them, since neither saves on its own.
for: The cross is where sin is dealt with: Lamb of God (John 1:29), atoning sacrifice (1 John 2:2).
'It is finished' (John 19:30): salvation completed on the cross.
The cross is the main Christian symbol and Holy Communion remembers Jesus' death.
against: 1 Corinthians 15:14: without the resurrection faith is in vain.
Many were crucified; only the resurrection shows Jesus is the Son of God and that death is defeated.
Easter and Sunday worship celebrate the resurrection; it gives hope of eternal life.
The Creeds link both: they are two halves of one act of salvation.
exam.conclusion: The resurrection is arguably more important because it gives meaning to the cross, but most Christians see them as inseparable parts of salvation.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the ascension of Jesus influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it gives Christians confidence when they pray. They believe that after the ascension Jesus is seated at the right hand of the Father, speaking for them, so they pray 'through Jesus Christ our Lord' and trust that God hears them. A second way is that it makes them carry on Jesus' mission. Just before he ascended, Jesus told his disciples to make disciples of all nations and promised the Holy Spirit's power, so Christians today share their faith and support mission, believing the Spirit helps them.
points: Confidence in prayer: Jesus intercedes for them at the Father's right hand
Carry on the Great Commission: evangelism and mission
Live ready for the second coming promised by the angels (Acts 1:11)
Belief that heaven is real and that life after death may be bodily
Celebrate Ascension Day and expect the Holy Spirit (Pentecost follows)

exam.q: Explain two different Christian beliefs about the resurrection of the dead. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that people will be raised with a body. Catholics, Orthodox and many other Christians believe God will give people a new, transformed body, not just a ghost-like existence. The Apostles' Creed says 'I believe in the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting'. This means many Christians treat the body with respect after death, and Catholics traditionally prefer burial, though cremation is allowed. A different belief is that the body will not be the same physical body we have now, or that only the soul lives on. Paul says the body 'is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body' (1 Corinthians 15:44). This means some Christians believe that what continues after death is the soul, which is non-physical and so cannot decay, and they see the funeral as saying goodbye to the body while the person lives on with God.
points: Bodily resurrection: a transformed physical body (Apostles' Creed)
Spiritual body / immortality of the soul (1 Corinthians 15:42-44)
Resurrection straight after death versus at the end of time when Jesus returns
Resurrection life is different from now (Matthew 22:30)
Application: burial customs, hope at funerals, respect for the body

exam.q: 'Belief in life after death is the most important Christian belief.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. Eternal life is the goal of the whole Christian faith: John 3:16 says God sent his Son so that whoever believes 'shall not perish but have eternal life'. Jesus promised, 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25), and the Apostles' Creed ends with 'the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting'. Belief in life after death gives Christians hope when loved ones die, removes the fear of death and shows that God's justice will finally be done. It also gives this life purpose, because people's choices now matter for eternity. This argument is strong because, without the hope of eternal life, many Christian teachings about salvation would have nothing to point towards.

However, other Christians argue that belief in God is more important. Life after death only makes sense if there is a God who is loving and powerful enough to raise the dead. The Trinity and the incarnation tell Christians who God is, and the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus are what make eternal life possible in the first place. Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15 bases the hope of resurrection on the fact that Christ has been raised, so Jesus' resurrection comes first.

Some Christians, especially liberal Christians, add that focusing on the afterlife can distract from living as Jesus taught now. Jesus said the greatest commandments are to love God and love your neighbour, and in the parable of the sheep and the goats people are judged on how they treat the needy in this life. If people only do good to reach heaven, their motive may be selfish.

In conclusion, I think life after death is extremely important, but not the most important belief. It depends on belief in God and in Jesus' resurrection, so those are more basic. Life after death is better seen as the result of Christian beliefs than their foundation.
for: Eternal life is the goal of salvation (John 3:16, John 11:25).
The Apostles' Creed ends with the life everlasting; it gives hope and removes fear of death.
It gives life purpose and shows God's justice will be done.
against: Belief in God (and the Trinity) comes first; the afterlife depends on God.
Jesus' resurrection is the basis of the hope of resurrection (1 Corinthians 15).
Jesus' greatest commandments focus on love now; doing good just to reach heaven may be selfish.
exam.conclusion: Life after death is very important but rests on belief in God and Jesus' resurrection, so it is a result of the foundations rather than the foundation itself.

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about God's judgement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that everyone will be judged by God. Christians believe that Jesus will return at the end of time and that no one can escape answering for how they have lived. The Apostles' Creed says Jesus 'will come to judge the living and the dead'. This means Christians take their choices seriously and confess their sins, because they will be accountable. A second belief is that people will be judged on how they treated others in need. In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46), Jesus says that whatever people did for 'one of the least of these' they did for him, and those who ignored the hungry and sick are sent away. This means Christians believe that faith must be shown in action, so many give to food banks, visit the sick or support charities such as Christian Aid.
points: Everyone will be judged; Jesus returns to judge the living and the dead (Apostles' Creed, 2 Corinthians 5:10)
Judgement on actions towards the needy (Matthew 25:31-46)
Judgement on faith in Jesus (John 14:6, John 3:36)
Particular judgement at death and final judgement at the end (Catholic)
God is just and merciful: repentance brings forgiveness
Application: moral living, charity, confession

exam.q: 'People should only be judged by God on their actions, not their beliefs.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Some Christians would agree with this statement. In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46), the people are not asked what they believed but whether they fed the hungry, welcomed strangers and visited prisoners. Even the 'sheep' did not realise they had been serving Jesus. James teaches that 'faith apart from works is dead' (James 2:26), and Jesus warned that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, but only those who do God's will (Matthew 7:21). This view seems fair, because people cannot always control what they believe, especially if they were never taught about Jesus, but they can choose how they treat others. Catholics stress that good works matter for salvation. This argument is strong because it is based directly on Jesus' own picture of judgement.

However, many Christians, especially Evangelical Protestants, disagree. Jesus said 'No one comes to the Father, except through me' (John 14:6), and John 3:36 says that whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Paul taught that people are saved 'by grace... through faith... not of works' (Ephesians 2:8-9), because everyone sins and no amount of good deeds can make up for it (Romans 3:23). If judgement were only about actions, salvation would be earned, and Jesus' death would be unnecessary. This argument is strong within Christian teaching, though some find it hard to accept that good people who do not believe could be lost.

Many Christians try to hold both together. They argue that real faith always shows itself in action, so actions reveal what someone truly believes. Belief and behaviour cannot be separated.

In conclusion, I disagree with the word 'only'. Christian teaching does not support judging on beliefs alone or on actions alone. The strongest view is that God judges the whole person, because faith that changes nothing is not real faith, and kind actions grow from a heart that trusts God.
for: Sheep and goats: people are judged on care for the needy, not stated belief (Matthew 25).
James 2:26: faith without works is dead; Matthew 7:21: doing God's will matters.
It seems fairer: people can choose actions more than beliefs, especially if never taught about Jesus.
against: John 14:6 and John 3:36: faith in Jesus is the way to the Father.
Ephesians 2:8-9: saved by grace through faith, not works; everyone sins (Romans 3:23).
If actions alone saved, salvation would be earned and Jesus' death unnecessary.
Real faith shows itself in action, so the two cannot be separated.
exam.conclusion: The word 'only' makes the statement too extreme: Christian teaching suggests God judges the whole person, with faith and actions linked.

exam.q: Explain two Christian beliefs about heaven. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model: One belief is that heaven is eternal life in the presence of God, free from all suffering. Revelation describes God wiping away every tear, with no more death, mourning, crying or pain (Revelation 21:4). This means Christians find comfort when loved ones die, believing that their suffering has ended and that they are with God. A second belief is that heaven is beyond what humans can imagine, so Christians disagree about what it is like. Some believe it is a real place, because Jesus said 'In my Father's house are many homes... I am going to prepare a place for you' (John 14:2). Others see it as a spiritual state of being close to God, since Paul says no eye has seen and no ear has heard what God has prepared (1 Corinthians 2:9). This means Christians focus less on details and more on trusting God and living faithfully now.
points: Eternal life with God, no suffering (Revelation 21:4)
A real place prepared by Jesus (John 14:2-3)
A spiritual state beyond imagination (1 Corinthians 2:9)
A reward for faith and/or good living (Matthew 25:46)
Catholics: purgatory may come first for some
Application: comfort at funerals, motivation to live well

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in original sin influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that it influences baptism. Catholics and many other Christians believe babies are born with original sin, so they have their children baptised as infants to wash it away and welcome them into God's family. A second way is that it makes Christians aware they need God's help. Because they believe everyone has a tendency to sin inherited from Adam and Eve, they confess their sins, pray for forgiveness and rely on God's grace rather than thinking they can be good enough on their own.
points: Infant baptism to cleanse original sin (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox)
Regular confession and prayer for forgiveness, e.g. the Lord's Prayer
Humility: relying on God's grace rather than their own goodness
Explains evil and suffering in the world, so they resist temptation
Some liberal Christians read it symbolically, so focus on choosing good

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the atonement influences Christians today. (4 marks)
exam.model: One way is that Christians take Holy Communion. They believe Jesus' death restored their relationship with God, so they regularly share bread and wine to remember his sacrifice and give thanks, as he told his disciples at the Last Supper. A second way is that they forgive others. Because they believe God has forgiven them at great cost through Jesus, they try to forgive people who hurt them, as they pray in the Lord's Prayer, 'forgive us our sins as we forgive those who sin against us'.
points: Take Holy Communion to remember Jesus' sacrifice
Forgive others because they have been forgiven
Feel free from guilt and live thankfully
Share the gospel so others can be reconciled to God
Wear a cross and keep Good Friday

exam.q: 'Jesus' death was necessary for humans to be saved.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Christian teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
exam.model:
Most Christians agree with this statement. They believe that sin separated humans from God, and that 'the wages of sin is death' (Romans 6:23). Since everyone has sinned (Romans 3:23), people could not repair the relationship themselves. Jesus, being both fully God and fully human, was the only one who could act for humanity as a sacrifice. John the Baptist called him 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29), and 1 Peter 2:24 says 'he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree'. Jesus himself said he came 'to give his life as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45), and he predicted his death as part of God's plan. This argument is strong, because the New Testament repeatedly presents Jesus' death as the means of atonement.

However, some people question whether it was truly necessary. If God is omnipotent and loving, he could simply forgive people, as the father in the parable of the prodigal son forgives his son without any payment (Luke 15). Some liberal Christians see Jesus' death mainly as an example of self-giving love that inspires people to change, rather than a payment God required. Others say that Jesus' life and teaching, or his resurrection, are just as important for salvation, because it is the resurrection that defeats death (1 Corinthians 15:14).

Christians would reply that sin is serious and that justice matters: forgiveness without any cost would make light of the harm sin does. They also argue that the cross shows how far God's love will go, 'while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8).

In conclusion, I agree with the statement from a Christian point of view. While God's power could in theory forgive without the cross, Christian teaching presents Jesus' death as the way God chose to show both his justice and love. However, it is best seen together with the resurrection, as one act of salvation.
for: Sin leads to death (Romans 6:23) and all have sinned (Romans 3:23), so humans could not save themselves.
Jesus is the Lamb of God (John 1:29), bore our sins (1 Peter 2:24), a ransom (Mark 10:45).
Jesus predicted his death as part of God's plan; it shows both God's justice and love (Romans 5:8).
against: An omnipotent, loving God could forgive freely, like the father in the prodigal son (Luke 15).
Liberal view: the cross is mainly a moral example, not a required payment.
The resurrection and Jesus' life and teaching are also central to salvation (1 Corinthians 15:14).
exam.conclusion: Within Christian teaching the cross is presented as necessary to show both justice and love, but it saves together with the resurrection rather than on its own.
